pass_a_gloss: [continued quotation] in us one may be. [Lemma 1 Cor 1:13] Is Christ divided (μεμέρισται)? Was Paul crucified for you? If another endured (ἀνέτλη) the cross for us, let us be called his; and if perchance we were baptized into another's calling/name (κλῆσιν), let that one have us, and let us inscribe (ἐπιγραψώμεθα) him savior and redeemer (λυτρωτήν); but if 'Christ died for our sins,' and with him alone we were buried with (συντεθάμμεθα) 'through baptism into death,' let him, he says, be rich in (πλουτείτω) the bought ones (ἠγορασμένους) himself; for we are saved through him and from him, who laid down his own life (ψυχήν) for us. [Lemma 1 Cor 1:17] For Christ did not send me to baptize but to evangelize. He was admittedly sent to proclaim Jesus to the Gentiles; but we say it is a work of the apostleship (ἀποστολῆς) to fulfill as in occasions and needs, if he should choose, also baptizing some. But lest he appear to spend the time of needing-to-preach on other pursuits (σπουδάσμασι), leaving it very well to those in the regions (κατὰ χώρας) and all appointed to oversight (ἐπισκοπήν) to do this as at leisure (ἐν σχολῇ), he rather evangelized himself, being entrusted with the need/ministry of the word (λόγου χρείαν) and having very precisely searched out (ἠκριβωκώς) the mystery of Christ; but as the divine Stephen, though appointed (προχειρισάμενος) deacon (διάκονον) of tables, did not dismiss the need to initiate into mysteries (μυσταγωγεῖν), so also the divine Paul, though set to evangelize the mystery of Christ, fulfilled at the time the need of baptism, the authority (ἐξουσίας) for both lying before him, and nothing excluding (ἐξείργοντος) if he chose to do this. [Lemma 1 Cor 1:20] Where wise? where scribe? where debater (συζητητής) of this age? To those thinking big on worldly wisdom and not admitting the faith, clearly that in Christ, the gospel is foolishness (μωρία); to us not so, far from it; for we are convinced (διατεθείμεθα) it is power of God, and way of salvation leading to sanctification, and guiding (παιδαγωγοῦσα) wisely to the full knowledge (ἐπίγνωσιν) of truth by abundant preachings. I think he now calls wise the orators (ῥήτορας), who by cleverness (δεινότητι) of speech always weaving the persuasive (πιθανόν) into falsehood, were eager to procure for it the seeming (δόκησιν) of truth; scribes I think the schoolmasters (γραμματιστάς) or grammarians, whose custom was to labor over the writings of poets and interpret to the young; debaters he says those used to word-fighting (λογομαχεῖν) and supposedly with precision examiners (βασανιστάς) of things, who by findings of concepts (ἐννοιῶν εὑρέσεσιν), as far as possible (ὡς ἑνί = ὡς ἔνι) to have what seems unimpeachable (ἀδιαβλήτως) on each matter proposed, pretend (ὑποκρίνονται) to seek truth, but not rightly, rather wholly carelessly; for they did not know the God of the universe, who framed (διεπήξατο) this whole by ineffable workings (ἐνεργείαις) without toil (ἀπονητί), and brought into being all things not being, by nodding only; so truly the wisdom of the world has been made foolish (μεμώραται). [Lemma 1 Cor 1:21] For since in the wisdom of God the world did not know through wisdom God, God was pleased through the foolishness of preaching to save the believers. Wisdom of God he names also human understanding (σύνεσιν) and eloquence (εὐγλωττίαν), that is, the flowery (ἀνθηρόν) of diction itself; to teach that God is maker of mind and supplier of prudence (φρονήσεως) and eloquence, even if some used them for what was not fitting; foolishness of preaching he calls the simplicity (ἁπλότητα) of words; for the divine disciples were laymen (ἰδιῶται) in speech, rich in knowledge (γνώσει). [Lemma 1 Cor 1:22] Since both Jews ask a sign and Greeks seek wisdom. On both counts true is Paul's word; for once when Christ was driving from the temple precincts (περιβόλων) those selling sheep and oxen, turtledoves and pigeons, and saying 'Do not make the house of my Father a house of trade (ἐμπορίου),' they countered 'What sign do you show us that you do these?' and 'Who gave you this authority?'; and some of the scribes came after very great display of signs, maliciously (φιλοκακούργως) saying 'Teacher, we want [continues].'
pass_b_english: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?” (1 Corinthians 1:13). If someone else endured the cross for us, let us be called his. If perhaps we were baptized into someone else’s name, let him have us, and let us enroll him as Savior and Redeemer. But if “Christ died for our sins” (1 Corinthians 15:3), and with him alone we have been “buried through baptism into death” (Romans 6:4), then let him, he says, possess those who have been bought. For we have been saved through him and by him, who laid down his own life for us (1 John 3:16).

“For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 1:17). He was admittedly sent to proclaim Jesus to the Gentiles. But we say that it also belongs to the work of an apostle to baptize some, as the occasion and need require, if he so chooses. So that he would not seem to spend the time owed to preaching on other pursuits, he very rightly left this to be done at leisure by those in each region and by all who were appointed to oversight. He himself preached the gospel instead, since he had been entrusted with the ministry of the word and had searched out the mystery of Christ with great precision. Yet just as the inspired Stephen, though appointed a servant of tables, did not set aside the duty of teaching the mysteries (Acts 6:2–5), so too the inspired Paul, though appointed to preach the mystery of Christ, also met the need for baptism when the time came. Authority for both lay before him, and nothing prevented him from doing it if he chose.

“Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?” (1 Corinthians 1:20). To those who pride themselves on worldly wisdom and do not accept the faith, clearly meaning faith in Christ, the gospel is foolishness. But it is not so with us; far from it. For we are convinced that it is the power of God (1 Corinthians 1:18), a way of salvation that leads to sanctification, and that by its abundant preaching it wisely guides us to the knowledge of the truth.

I for my part think that here he calls the orators “wise,” who by the cleverness of their speeches always wove persuasion into falsehood and strove to win for it the appearance of truth. By “scribes” I think he means the schoolmasters or grammarians, whose custom it was to labor over the writings of the poets and to explain them to the young. By “debaters” he means those who are used to fighting over words and who, supposedly with precision, put things to the test. Through the concepts they devise they pretend to seek the truth, that is, whatever seems, as far as possible, to stand beyond reproach on each question set before them. But they do not do it rightly at all; rather, they do it with utter carelessness. For they have not known the God of all, who without toil framed this whole universe by ineffable workings, and by a mere nod brought into being all things that were not. So the wisdom of the world has truly been made foolish (1 Corinthians 1:20).

“For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). He calls even human understanding and eloquence, that is, the very bloom of style, “the wisdom of God,” to teach that God is the maker of the mind and the giver of good sense and eloquence, even if some have used them for ends they should not. By “the foolishness of the preaching” he means the plainness of the words. For the inspired disciples were unskilled in speech but rich in knowledge (2 Corinthians 11:6).

“For Jews ask for a sign, and Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:22). Paul’s statement is true on both counts. Once, when Christ was driving out of the temple courts those who sold sheep and oxen, turtledoves and pigeons, and saying, “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” (John 2:14–16), they retorted, “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” (John 2:18), and, “Who gave you this authority?” (Matthew 21:23). Some of the scribes also came to him, after a very great display of signs, and said with malice, “Teacher, we wish […]” (Matthew 12:38).

The middle form is read in a passive sense of Stephen.
ὡς ἑνί is read as ὡς ἔνι.

αὐτοῦ καὶ λεγώμεθα is 'let us be called his' (possession), and 'too' read as an added comparison; τὸν τῶν ὅλων Θεόν rendered 'the God of all' to avoid the repeated 'universe ... whole universe'. Second review: ἁγιασμόν is 'sanctification', as in u01-open, not 'holiness'; in the debaters clause 'so as to reach' added a purpose the Greek lacks: τὸ ... ἀδιαβλήτως ἔχειν δοκοῦν stands in apposition to τὴν ἀλήθειαν ('they pretend to seek the truth, that is, whatever seems beyond reproach'), with ὡς ἔνι 'as far as possible'.
